title: Indra Asks About Deep Sleep
hookLine: Indra studies the self for a hundred and one years and nearly quits over deep sleep; the morning's 'I slept well' says someone was there
carry: the self is the witness, even in deep sleep
tomorrow: Kumbhakarna woke and told the king the truth. then what?

lines: THE KING OF THE GODS, A STUDENT.
I SEE NO GOOD IN THIS.
cards: Indra, king of the gods, wants to know the self. In the Chandogya Upanishad he goes to Prajapati, the creator, and lives with him as a student for thirty-two years. He's taught, he leaves, he doubts, he comes back.
It happens again. The third time, Prajapati points him to deep, dreamless sleep. And Indra, halfway home, stops on the road.
Paraphrased: in that state a person doesn't even know, 'this is me.' It's as if he's gone to nothing. I see no good in this. Today, the king of the gods against the gap in the night.

teach.h: A HUNDRED AND ONE YEARS FOR ONE TEACHING
teach.b: Prajapati doesn't scold him. He says: stay five more years. Indra's whole stay comes to a hundred and one years, the text says, for one teaching.
And the teaching, paraphrased: this body is mortal, held by death, but it's the dwelling of a self that is deathless and without a body. Another school asks the same question.
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras count sleep among the mind's five movements: a turning that rests on absence. And the commentary credited to Vyasa notices the morning.

teach.h: I SLEPT WELL: SOMEONE WAS THERE
teach.b: On waking, a person says, I slept well, my mind is clear. Or, I slept badly, my mind is dull. You can't remember what never happened to you, so something was there.
Here is the teaching, named plainly.

Vedanta teachers call it the witness, sakshi: the self, atman, that sees waking, sees dreams, and is present even when there is nothing to see. Many teachers read the morning's 'I slept well' as the witness's fingerprint.
You can't look at it, which is exactly why Indra kept missing it: it's the one doing the looking.

teach.h: YOU AREN'T YOUR MOODS OR NIGHTS
teach.b: That's why, in this teaching, you aren't your moods or your nights. Light and heavy, clear and dull, they come and go, and the witness sees them all.
And as with every day in this lens: the texts describe the mind; they don't diagnose sleep. Heavy nights and dull mornings for a long stretch are a conversation for a doctor.

how: Vedanta teachers read Indra's long stay with Prajapati as a lesson in how to look for the self, and point to deep sleep and the morning's 'I slept well' to teach atman as the witness, sakshi; students of the Yoga Sutras learn sleep as one of the five vrittis.

o: a blank: the self switches off each night and restarts
the witness, present through waking, dream and deep sleep
a state where the self is lost until a guru wakes it

games.q: Indra and the witness — tap the pairs.
p: a student of Prajapati for 101 years
I slept well, my mind is clear
the morning's memory of the night
the witness, the self that sees

s: Indra was satisfied the first time Prajapati taught him
he doubted, came back, and doubted again. the stay came to a hundred and one years.
the Yoga Sutras count sleep among the mind's movements
right knowing, error, imagination, sleep and memory: five turnings, and sleep is one.
in Vedanta, the witness is something you can look at, like an object
it's the one doing the looking, which is why Indra kept missing it.

games.q: you're Indra. years of study, and the teaching ends at deep sleep, where you don't even know 'this is me'. what do you do?
o: go back to Prajapati and say, i see no good in this.
games.why: Indra goes back with his doubt. Prajapati keeps him five more years and teaches the deathless self that the body only houses.

practice: Go back to last night's sleep, not the hours but the quality, light or heavy, clear or tangled, and find one honest word for it. Then notice: something just remembered a night you were supposedly absent for.
Rest a few breaths as the one who notices, not as the night. If you pray, give thanks for whatever rest there was.

wordCard.voice: Sleep. For Indra, a gap that looked like nothing; in the Yoga Sutras, a turning of the mind remembered in the morning; for Vedanta, a night the witness sees. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit sakshi: witness. Vedanta's name for the self that sees waking, dream and deep sleep.

carryVoice: Your line: the self is the witness, even in deep sleep. Indra waited a hundred and one years for it. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7–8.10 (Indra and Virochana go to Prajapati; thirty-two years; the self in the water, then the dreamer; Indra doubts and returns)

Chandogya Upanishad 8.11.1–3 (the self in deep sleep; Indra: he does not know himself as 'I am he', as if gone to destruction, I see no good in this; five more years; one hundred and one years in all)
Chandogya Upanishad 8.12.1 (this body is mortal, held by death; it is the support of the deathless, bodiless self)
Yoga Sutras 1.6 (the five vrittis: pramana, viparyaya, vikalpa, nidra, smriti)
Yoga Sutras 1.10 (sleep is the vritti resting on the experience of absence)
Vyasa's Bhashya on Yoga Sutras 1.10 (on waking: I slept well, my mind is clear; I slept badly, my mind is dull; the memory shows sleep was experienced)
